scenes.title: Jacqueline Metzler and Roger Shepard timing a participant comparing two 10-cube 3D perspective blocks beside the ruler-straight 0-to-180° graph
scenes.era: 1971, Stanford University cognitive psychology laboratory, California

layout.description: Sunlit 1971 Stanford laboratory featuring a tachistoscopic viewing hood and white display screen showing a crisp black-line pair of asymmetric 10-cube 3D perspective arms rotated 120 degrees apart, flanked by Same/Different response levers and a large plotted linear graph.

positions.where: seated at the viewing console with hands poised on left/right response levers, tilting head subtly by a few degrees while mentally rotating the right-hand 10-cube block

positions.who: Jacqueline Metzler & Roger Shepard (mannequins in 1971 blazer and collared shirt)
positions.where: standing beside the digital millisecond counter and plotted Science graph showing the razor-straight 1s-to-4.5s line

props.name: physical white 10-cube wooden reference models
props.period_detail: two real L-and-elbow sculptures glued from ten white wooden cubes (one congruent pair, one chiral mirror twin) resting on the bench
props.physical_behavior: let viewers immediately see how 3D rotation differs from a mirror twin

props.name: twin-circle stimulus display screen
props.period_detail: two crisp white circles framing isometric 10-cube line drawings rotated 120 degrees in depth
props.physical_behavior: requires exactly ~3.0 seconds before the 'Same' lever clicks

props.name: linear 0°-to-180° reaction-time chart
props.period_detail: clean black-on-white graph plotting 20° steps in a straight diagonal line (~60° per second)
props.physical_behavior: proves 3D depth and 2D flat curves match

actions.verb_sequence: reveals two 10-cube shapes rotated 120° in depth -> Participant's head tilts slightly across 3.0 seconds -> right hand pulls the 'Same' lever cleanly
plots the 3.0-second data point squarely onto the straight 120° diagonal line

reactions.reaction: picks up the two white wooden 10-cube models and turns one smoothly by 120° to match the screen
relaxes after locking the 3D shapes into alignment

scenes.wardrobe: 1971 Stanford academic wear: Metzler in tailored wool blazer and blouse; Shepard in Oxford shirt and tweed jacket; participant in ribbed knit sweater.
scenes.lighting: Clean high-key California laboratory daylight illuminating the white 10-cube sculptures and graph.
scenes.recognition_hook: Every extra sixty degrees between two ten-cube shapes adds one exact second on the stopwatch — proving your mind physically rotates objects through every angle in between.

key_visual.description: a 1971 Stanford lab desk with white 10-cube 3D block models, a twin-circle perspective display, response levers, and a straight diagonal 0-to-180 degree reaction-time graph

scenes.title: Congruent twin vs impossible chiral mirror-image block

layout.description: Close high-key tabletop view of three white wooden 10-cube sculptures: Standard, Rotated Twin, and Mirror Enantiomorph.

positions.where: rotating the congruent twin smoothly into alignment, then trying the mirror twin which points the opposite way

props.name: three 10-cube white wooden sculptures
props.physical_behavior: demonstrate why mirror twins can never superimpose

actions.verb_sequence: aligns the first pair cleanly -> rotates the mirror twin 180° showing the final elbow juts the wrong way

reactions.reaction: notes just 3.2 percent error across 1,600 trials

scenes.recognition_hook: Like a left and right glove, chiral 10-cube mirror twins never align no matter how far you spin them.

scenes.title: Hand-turning interference proving premotor involvement

layout.description: Clean test station where a participant turns a smooth wooden dial counterclockwise with one hand while trying to mentally rotate a block clockwise on screen.

positions.where: turning a tabletop dial opposite the screen block's shortest path, causing a visible brief pause

props.name: rotary wooden hand dial
props.physical_behavior: demonstrates motor-imagery overlap in premotor cortex

actions.verb_sequence: turns dial counterclockwise while rotating image clockwise -> millisecond counter ticks slower

scenes.recognition_hook: Turning your physical hand the opposite way slows down your 'mind's eye' because both share premotor circuits.

scenes.title: Architect rotating a physical white foam model in hand to free working memory

layout.description: Sunlit studio table where an architect picks up a white 3D foam stair-core model and rotates it in two seconds instead of staring blankly at flat plans.

positions.where: turning a crisp white foam architectural model smoothly in both hands

props.name: white 3D architectural massing model
props.physical_behavior: solves a tricky stairwell clearance instantly

actions.verb_sequence: lifts physical model -> turns 120° in hand -> marks the exact fit on the drawing

scenes.recognition_hook: Turning a quick physical sketch or model in your hands frees your parietal workspace for bigger decisions.
